# Fed’s June FOMC: New Fed Chair, New Fed Incoming

Fed held rates steady; it was a notable meeting as Kevin Warsh’s first FOMC as chair.

June 24, 2026

While there was no surprise with the U.S. Federal Reserve (the “Fed”) holding policy rates steady this week, it was an exciting Fed meeting because this was Kevin Warsh’s first Fed Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting as Fed Chair. Warsh did not waste time and announced a major revamping of the Fed’s operating framework, starting with the long‑overdue end to relying on forward guidance. From now on, markets will largely be on their own in figuring out the implications of economic and financial developments and what they entail for the Fed’s policy outlook. This will make the guessing game around the Fed more interesting. It is unclear whether clear market volatility will increase simply because the Fed is no longer holding markets’ hands.

# Four key takeaways from Jerome Powell's final rate decision as Fed chair

29 April 2026

Archie Mitchell Business reporter

Getty Images

The Federal Reserve has held US interest rates steady after what was expected to be Jerome Powell's final meeting as chair.

Hours after his successor Kevin Warsh won the backing of a key Senate committee to take up the role next month, Powell announced the Fed's rate would stay between 3.5% and 3.75%.

It followed continued pressure from US President Donald Trump on the Fed to lower interest rates, with the Trump having criticised Powell throughout his presidency.

Warsh is expected to face the same pressure from the president, but has vowed to uphold the central bank's independence when he takes over from Powell.

# The Fed, under new chair Kevin Warsh, held rates at 3.5% to 3.75% and raised its 2026 inflation outlook to 3.6%

 Warren Cohen 3 months ago 3 months ago 0 9 mins 

 Kucuktezcan/Freepik 

Borrowers, savers, and bond traders all got the same answer from the Federal Reserve on June 17, 2026: no change. The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to keep the federal funds rate at 3.5% to 3.75%, the first rate decision under Chair Kevin Warsh, who took office less than a month earlier. Alongside the hold, the committee released updated economic projections showing a 2026 inflation outlook of 3.6%, measured by the PCE price index, and declared in its official statement that “inflation remains elevated.” The decision sets up a tense stretch for markets adjusting to a new Fed leader who has signaled less hand-holding on future rate moves.

# Warsh's First FOMC Press Conference: The Dot Plot Is the Signal 

SixPoint Spotlight

Jun 29, 2026

Executive Summary

The FOMC held rates at 3.50–3.75% on a unanimous 12-0 vote. The decision was not the event — the dot plot and press conference were. The June 17 SEP confirmed the hawkish shift: the 2026 median dot moved to 3.8% (from 3.4% in March), with 9 of 18 members projecting at least one hike by year-end and 6 projecting two. PCE inflation revised to 3.6% at year-end (was 2.7%). Warsh formally dispensed with forward guidance, releasing a shorter statement that removed easing-bias language entirely. His tone: the commitment to price stability is “strong, unanimous, and unambiguous.” Markets now price a 60.7% probability of a hike in October. The next move is a hike, not a cut — and the EIBOR-linked GCC and EM borrowing cost implications activate immediately.
